## How-Tos

These how-tos assume you've worked through [Get Started](start-here.qmd) — you'll be
comfortable loading jstats, using `juse()` and `jload()`, and running the basic
functions. Each one stands on its own, so read whichever you need; for now,
[Get Started](start-here.qmd) is the place to begin.

The articles below are on the way. They go beyond the Get Started on-ramp and point
toward the fuller treatment in the books.

## Using your own data

*Coming soon* — the bridge from the practice datasets to a file of your own: opening
an Excel, CSV, or commercial-software file, keeping it in a data folder, and taking
a first look with `jscreen()`.

## Working with data from commercial statistical software

*Coming soon* — importing and working with data from SPSS, Stata, and SAS, including
value and variable labels and the different missing-value conventions.

## Reading jstats output: Case Processing and Missing data

*Coming soon* — not how to interpret the statistics, but how to read the accounting
printed above them: the Case Processing lines and tables that say how many cases an
analysis used and which were set aside, and the Missing data breakdown that shows
where each variable's missing values went.

## Recoding and relabeling variables

*Coming soon* — reverse-coding an item, collapsing categories, and fixing variable
and value labels with `jrecode()` and `jrelabel()`, keeping the original column
intact.

## Text answers into coded variables

*Coming soon* — turning a column of words ("Yes", "No", "Don't know") from a
spreadsheet or survey export into a labeled, coded variable with `jencode()`.

## Building and checking a scale

*Coming soon* — combining Likert items into a scale and checking its reliability with
Cronbach's alpha.

## Working on part of your data

*Coming soon* — analyzing a subgroup with `jsubset()`, and using `jcomplete()` so a
set of analyses all run on the same cases.

## Comparing groups

*Coming soon* — t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and cross-tabulations with `jt()`, `jaov()`,
and `jcrosstab()`: one formula style for all three, how to read what comes back, and
the Welch versions of the t-test and ANOVA (`welch = TRUE`), which do not assume
equal variances.

## Regression with categorical predictors

*Coming soon* — linear and logistic regression with `jlm()` and `jlogistic()`.
`jdummy()` is the quick way in for a categorical variable: register its dummy coding
and reference category once, and it goes into a model by name — no building dummy
variables by hand, and no converting to base R's factors.

## Handling missing values across platforms

*Coming soon* — what survives when data move between SPSS, Stata, SAS, and R: round
trips between formats, converting declarations from one convention to another,
missing-value ranges, and the SAS interchange format. Declaring missing values in the
first place is covered in
*[Telling jstats about missing values](missing-values.qmd)*.
